witness.text:
sitting around

comparisons.rationale: Rachel's year-3 portfolio is stated as about $80,000, but $51,000 plus 36 x $1,400 is $101,400 with zero return and about $118,800 at 7%.
comparisons.uncertainty: Arithmetic verified in this session.

witness.text:
he's got maybe
50,000 in equity

comparisons.rationale: The down payment alone is $41,500, and principal repaid after 36 payments on $373,500 at 6.5% is about $13,400, so equity is at least about $54,900 before any appreciation and about $106,700 with the video's own 4% appreciation. The stated $50,000 is below even the zero-appreciation figure. After a 5.5% exit toll the owner is about -$20K against the $51,500 put in at zero appreciation and about +$29K at 4%, so "almost nothing" fits neither case exactly.
comparisons.uncertainty: Arithmetic verified in this session; equity before selling costs.

witness.text:

comparisons.rationale: $415,000 on $41,500 down is 10-to-1 leverage, not 5-to-1.
comparisons.uncertainty: Arithmetic verified.

witness.text:
her portfolio lands in that
same range,5 to $600,000

comparisons.rationale: With a flat $1,400/month and $51,000 over 20 years, $500-600K requires about 3-3.5% a year; at 5% the result is about $714K and at the video's own 7% about $935K, while Brian's equity is about $542K at 3% appreciation. The video also says Brian's "mortgage is nearly dead" at year 20, but about $207,900 (56%) of the $373,500 loan is still owed. The "same ballpark" conclusion fails on the video's own assumptions. (The monthly gap would shrink as rent rises, which lowers Rachel's figure but is not modelled.)
comparisons.uncertainty: Arithmetic verified; scenario assumptions simplified.

witness.text:
His monthly principal
and interest come to roughly $2,360

comparisons.rationale: $373,500 at 6.5% over 30 years is $2,360.77/month; total interest $476,379, which exceeds the $415,000 price ("nearly the entire price a second time" understates it). Property tax ($346/month at 1%), the 5% rule ($1,729/month) and the "$1,400 gap" ($3,400 less $2,015) also reconstruct.
comparisons.uncertainty: Verified arithmetic. Payment crossover to majority principal is month 233 (year 19.4), not "around year 18".

witness.text:

comparisons.uncertainty: The 5% rule is a rule of thumb, not a verified method.

financial_checks.result: $346; $1,729; $2,360 + 350 + 200 + 150 + ~350 maintenance is about $3,410; gap about $1,395. Holds (the later "$2,300" payment is a small slip).
CONTRADICTED: $101,400 contributed with no growth; $113,500 at 5%; $118,800 at 7%.
CONTRADICTED: $54,900 with zero appreciation ($41,500 + $13,400 principal); $106,700 at 4% appreciation.

financial_checks.claim: Year 20: Brian equity "north of $500,000" and Rachel "5 to $600,000", same ballpark
financial_checks.result: Brian: $409K / $542K / $701K at 2% / 3% / 4% appreciation. Rachel (flat $1,400, $51,000 start): $387K at 0%, $552K at 3%, $714K at 5%, $935K at 7%. The video's own 7% real return puts Rachel far ahead; the quoted range corresponds to ~3-3.5%. Also: remaining loan balance at year 20 is about $207,900 (56%), not "nearly dead".

financial_checks.claim: Rent rising "about 4% a year", "toward nearly three" thousand
financial_checks.result: $2,000 at 4% is $2,960 at year 10 and $4,382 at year 20; "nearly three" is the year-10 figure.

financial_checks.claim: Home prices about 1% a year real; stocks about 7% real; break-even about 6 years; about 1 in 10 itemize; "nearly 40 times" owner versus renter; median renter has a few hundred to a couple thousand invested
financial_checks.result: Not re-verified. The 1%/7% figures match the figures in the sibling video -DIT32sBkAk (0.3-1% and 7.3%), which is not independent evidence.

strengths: Controlled two-character comparison with identical inputs and a clear time-based spine.
Both outcomes framed fairly; the two deciding variables (appreciation rate, whether the renter invests) are the right ones.
Callbacks and humour strengthen retention design.
weaknesses: Several year-3 and year-20 scenario figures do not follow from stated inputs, and the final "same ballpark" conclusion fails on the video's own 7% assumption.
Hook promises a surprising winner that the ending withdraws.
Mid-argument community pitch; stored transcript truncated at the end.
contradictions: 5% rule says buying is ahead at $2,000 rent, but the narrative has the renter ahead and "a coin flip".
"Five to six percent" exit cost and "$2,300 / $2,360" payment slips.
Rachel's portfolio $80K at year 3 below zero-growth contributions.
"His mortgage is nearly dead" at year 20 with 56% of the loan still owed.
improvement_opportunities: Show Rachel's and Brian's balance sheets at years 3, 10 and 20 as one on-screen table built from the stated inputs, with the assumption (appreciation and return) printed under each.
Rename the promise: replace "the winner is not who you think" with a promise the ending keeps, or end with the conditional decision rule earlier.
Put the community pitch after the two-variable payoff, not before it.
Give the thumbnail one number or a tension line ("20 years, same house") so it carries a curiosity gap beyond the generic question.
